sections.title: Page 1 · The Contemporary World Reviewer
sections.body:
The Contemporary World Reviewer

I. Introduction to Globalization

   ●  Definition: Globalization is the ever-increasing interconnectedness and
      interdependence among individuals, states, and nations. It encompasses
      economic integration, cultural exchange, and the shrinking of geographical
       distance.
   ●  Philosophical Perspectives:
        ○  Hyperglobalist: Believes in a profound, irreversible transformation creating
            a single "borderless world" where national governments lose power to
              global markets and supranational organizations.
        ○  Skeptic/Anti-Globalist: Argues globalization is not unprecedented but a
             continuation of Western internationalization. The nation-state endures.
               Critics like Walden Bello view it as a neo-liberal ideology that exacerbates
               inequality.
        ○  Transformationalist: Believes the state is not declining but being
             reconfigured to adapt to global forces. Emphasizes "glocalization" (global
             forces interacting with local contexts).

II. The Structures of Globalization

Global Economy

   ●  Global Trade: Dominated by Global Value Chains (GVCs). For example, the
       Philippine electronics and electrical machinery sector accounts for nearly half of
        total exports, integrating the country into the global tech GVC.
   ●  Global Finance: The movement of money, capital, and assets across borders. The
      Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) manages this by liberalizing foreign exchange
       rules to mobilize resources while maintaining strong Gross International Reserves.
   ●  Global Labor/Migration: The cross-border movement of people driven by wage
        differentials. For the Philippines, this is heavily characterized by Overseas Filipino
      Workers (OFWs) whose remittances bolster the national GDP.

sections.title: Page 2 · Market Integration
sections.body:
Market Integration

   ●  Corporate Market Integration:
        ○  Horizontal: Gaining control of competitors at the same production level
                (e.g., Ayala Corp acquiring Zalora).
        ○  Vertical: Controlling different stages of production or marketing (e.g., San
            Miguel Corp owning farms, feed mills, and meat shops).
        ○  Conglomerate: Combining unrelated enterprises to diversify risk (e.g., SM
             Investments Corp operating in retail, banking, and property).
   ●  Spatial Market Integration: Examines how efficiently price signals transmit across
      geographic regions. In the Philippines, despite logistics challenges across the
       archipelago, efficient rice price transmission ensures food security by moving
      supply to areas with shortages.

III. The Structures of Globalization

Global Interstate System

   ●  Core Concepts: The framework of cooperating and contending sovereign states,
      founded on the Peace of Westphalia (1648). A state is a political community with
        territory, population, government, and sovereignty. A nation is an "imagined
      community" sharing culture and history.
   ●  Philippine Challenges:
        ○  External Intervention: The West Philippine Sea dispute involves asserting
             sovereignty under UNCLOS against China, highlighting the limits of legal
             sovereignty without great power support.
        ○  Economic: Adhering to the laws of neoliberal capitalism limits the state's
                ability to impose protectionist tariffs.

Contemporary Global Governance

   ●  Definition & Actors: Managing collective global affairs in the absence of a single
      world government. Key actors include Intergovernmental Organizations (IGOs like
       the WTO), Transnational NGOs (like Amnesty International), and binding treaties
        (like the Paris Agreement).

   ●  Philippine Experience (Global): The UN system supports PH development (SDGs)

IV. A World of Regions

Global Divides

   ●  The Divide (North vs. South): Used to describe vast disparities in wealth, power,
      and development.
        ○  Global North: Wealthy, industrialized, technologically advanced nations that
              inherited colonial wealth (e.g., US, Western Europe).
        ○  Global South: Developing or newly industrialized agrarian/commodity-
            dependent nations with a shared history of colonialism.

Asian Regionalism

   ●  Definition: The process of increasing economic, political, and socio-cultural
       integration among Asian nations. Unlike the EU's legally binding political design,
      Asian Regionalism is primarily market-driven through trade and production supply
       chains.
   ●  The "ASEAN Way": A unique approach to cooperation characterized by non-
       interference in internal affairs, consensus-based decision-making (quiet
       diplomacy), and informality.
   ●  Philippine Role: As a founding member of ASEAN (1967), the Philippines
       participates in economic integration (like AFTA and RCEP) and utilizes collective
      diplomacy via forums like the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) to assert national
       interests and manage geopolitical tensions.The Philippine Position: Universally
      categorized in the Global South due to economic dependency on OFWs/exports
      and a colonial legacy. However, it exhibits some "Northern" nuances, like a high
        literacy rate and a globally competitive IT-BPM sector.

sections.title: Page 1 · GNED 10 Midterm Reviewer
sections.body:
GNED 10 Midterm Reviewer

IV. Gender and Work

   ●  Gender Gaps: The IMF notes that gender inequality in the labor market causes
      economic losses due to the misallocation of women's labor. In the Philippines,
     women are more likely to hold lower-quality or vulnerable employment.
      Furthermore, women's heavy responsibility for unpaid domestic work limits their
        ability to engage in paid work on the same terms as men.
   ●  Sex-Typing: This is the belief that men and women are suited for specific jobs
      based on biological sex. For example, engineering and mechanics are seen as
       "masculine," while teaching and nursing are "feminine." Parents strongly impact
       early sex-typing.
   ●  Discrimination:
        ○  Access Discrimination: Difficulty getting hired in a particular field based on
            sex (e.g., fewer women in judicial roles).
        ○  Treatment Discrimination: When a woman earns less (pay gap) or receives
            fewer promotion opportunities than a male co-worker despite having the
          same qualifications and performance.
   ●  Pregnancy: Mothers face the "mommy tax" or maternal wall. Pregnant women are
       often stereotyped as delicate, overly emotional, or pitied. Their commitment is
      questioned, and companies often view maternity as an expense.
   ●  Work-Family Balance: Bridging the gender gap in the workplace requires equal
      pay, eliminating discrimination, and promoting work-family balance. This includes
      recognizing that women do the bulk of unpaid household work and providing
      adequate maternity protection and paid parenting leaves.

V. Gender and School

   ●  Gender Socialization: The family and the school are the two main pillars of
       socialization. Gender socialization is the process through which individuals learn to
      behave, feel, and think according to the forms deemed appropriate for their sex by
       society. Schools often unintentionally reinforce traditional stereotypes.

●  Gender-Responsive Education: Schools should deliberately build proper gender
      education to benefit society. Educators committed to egalitarianism should
      promote cross-gender interaction, expose pupils to counter-stereotypic models,
      and teach challenges to gender harassment.
   ●  Teacher Bias: Teachers interact with boys 10 to 30 percent more often. They also
      tend to use "public talk" (talking from a distance) with boys and "private talk" with
         girls. Furthermore, teachers tend to praise boys for correct knowledge while
      overlooking their wrong answers, and criticize girls for incorrect answers while
      overlooking their right ones.

      segregated contexts (like single-sex schools) and instead enhance co-educational
       schools' promotion of egalitarian attitudes. Teachers also need explicit policy-
      backed training to recognize and confront their own explicit and implicit biases.

Pickleball is a paddle sport that can be
played indoors or outdoors, it is a hybrid of
Badminton, Tennis, and Table-tennis. It can
be played as single (one player per side) or
doubles (two players per side).

•  Initially , families played Pickleball in their backyards on a hard
   surface, on driveways, and on residential dead-end streets.
•  Since the mid-1970’s, Pickleball has grown and expanded from a family
    activity game to paddle court sport, with formalized rules. Now, over 20 yrs
    later, Pickleball is played in thousands of school P.E programs, parks and
   recreation centers, correctional facilities, camps, YMCAs, and retirement
   communities. This sport  is becoming very popular among active senior
   adults at community centers and is growing in popularity on high school and
   college campuses.

BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS

Serving
•  Must be made diagonally crosscourt.
•  Must land in the opponent's appropriate service court.
•  Must clear the non-volley zone.
•   Is made from behind the baseline.
•  In traditional serving, is performed using an underhand
   motion.

sections.title: Page 17 · BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS
sections.body:
BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS

Two-Bounce Rule
One of pickleball's most important rules is the two-bounce rule.
After the serve:
• The receiving team must allow the ball to bounce before
   returning it.
• The serving team must then allow that return to bounce
  before hitting it.
After these two required bounces, players may volley the ball.

sections.title: Page 18 · BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS
sections.body:
BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS

Non-Valley Zone/Kitchen
A player may enter the kitchen but cannot
volley the ball while standing in it or touching
its boundary line. A player also cannot volley
and then have momentum carry them into the
non-volley zone.

sections.title: Page 19 · BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS
sections.body:
BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS

Ball In or Out
A ball  is in  if  it lands inside the appropriate
boundary lines.
A ball that lands outside the relevant boundary
is out.

sections.title: Page 20 · BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS
sections.body:
BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS

Ball In or Out
An important exception  is the  kitchen  line:
because the non-volley zone extends to the
inside edge of the court, a ball landing on the
non-volley-zone line during a serve is considered
a fault.

sections.title: Page 21 · BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS
sections.body:
BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS
Faults
A fault can occur when:
• The ball goes out of bounds.
• The ball does not clear the net.
• A player violates the serving requirements.
• A player volleys while violating the non-volley-zone
   rule.
• A player violates other applicable rules.

sections.title: Page 22 · BASIC RULES AND REGULATIONS

Scoring
Under traditional scoring, only the serving side
scores points. A point is won when the serving team
wins the rally.
Games are commonly played to 11 points, and a
team must win by 2 points. Competitive formats may
use different scoring systems or game lengths.

BASIC SKILLS

1. Ready Position
• Keep your feet about shoulder-width apart.
• Bend your knees slightly and maintain a
  balanced stance.
• Hold the paddle in front of your body.
•  Stay prepared to move in any direction.

sections.title: Page 32 · BASIC SKILLS

2. Footwork and Movement
•  Move quickly and maintain balance while playing.
•  Use small adjustment steps when approaching the
    ball.
•  Avoid crossing your feet during lateral movement.
•  Proper footwork helps players reach the ball and
   maintain good positioning.

sections.title: Page 33 · BASIC SKILLS
sections.body:

3. Hand-Eye Coordination
• Track the  ball  carefully from the
 opponent's paddle to your own.
• Coordinate your paddle movement
 with the ball's speed and direction.

sections.title: Page 34 · BASIC SKILLS
sections.body:

4. Serving
•  Start each rally by serving diagonally
   into the opponent's service court.
•  Focus on  accuracy,  consistency, and
   proper placement.

sections.title: Page 35 · BASIC SKILLS
sections.body:
BASIC SKILLS
5. Returning the Serve
• Allow  the  serve  to  bounce  before
  returning it.
• Aim to return the ball deep into the
  opponent's court when possible.

sections.title: Page 36 · BASIC SKILLS
sections.body:

6. Dinking
• A dink is a soft shot that lands in or near
  the opponent's non-volley zone.
•  It is used to slow down the rally and
  create opportunities.

sections.title: Page 37 · BASIC SKILLS

7. Volleys
• A volley is hitting the ball before it bounces.
•  Volleys are commonly used when players
  are positioned near the net.
•  Players must observe the non-volley-zone
   rules when volleying.

9. Groundstrokes
• A groundstroke is a shot made after the ball
  bounces.
• The most common groundstrokes are the

sections.title: Page 41 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:
BASIC STROKES

1. Forehand Stroke
•  The paddle is swung on the dominant side of the body.
•  For a right-handed player, the stroke is generally made
  on the right side.
•  Rotate the body and swing the paddle forward.
•  Follow through toward the intended target.
•  Commonly used for groundstrokes, drives, and returns.

sections.title: Page 42 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:
BASIC STROKES

2. Backhand Stroke
• The paddle is swung across the opposite side of the
  body.
• For a right-handed player, the backhand is generally
  made on the left side.
• Turn the shoulders and prepare the paddle early.
• Swing forward while maintaining control.
• Can be performed with one hand or two hands.

sections.title: Page 43 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:
BASIC STROKES
3. Serve
• The serve begins each rally.
• The  traditional serve  is performed  using an
  underhand motion.
• The ball must travel diagonally across the court.
• The serve should be controlled and accurate
  rather than simply powerful.

sections.title: Page 44 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:
BASIC STROKES
4. Return of Serve
•  The receiving player allows the serve to bounce
   before hitting it.
• A deep return  is commonly used to give the
   receiving team time to move toward the net.
•  Focus on control, accuracy, and placement.

sections.title: Page 45 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:
BASIC STROKES
5. Dink
• A  soft,  controlled  shot  that  lands  in  the
  opponent's non-volley zone.
•  Usually performed with a  short and  gentle
  paddle motion.
•  Used  to  create  opportunities  and  prevent
  opponents from attacking aggressively.

sections.title: Page 46 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:

6. Drive
• A drive is a faster and more powerful
  groundstroke.
•  It is usually hit after the ball bounces.
• Can be used to put pressure on opponents
  or force a weak return.

sections.title: Page 47 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:

7. Volley
• A volley is hit before the ball bounces.
•  It is often used close to the net.
• Requires quick reaction, good paddle
  positioning, and control.

sections.title: Page 48 · BASIC STROKES
sections.body:
BASIC STROKES
8. Lob
• A lob sends the ball high and deep over
  the opponent.
•  It can be used offensively or defensively.
•  Effective placement is more important
  than excessive power.

summary: Table tennis became an Olympic sport in 1988.

Core strokes include backhand, forehand, push, block and smash.
A game generally goes to 11 with at least a two-point lead.

12th Century AD – The game
of table tennis probably
descended from the the game
of “Royal Tennis” (also known
as Real Tennis or Court
Tennis), which was played in
the medieval era.

sections.title: Page 4 · HISTORY

1880- Ping-pong started in
Victorian England during an
indoor parlor game. Wealthy
upper-class families used dining
tables, books for a net, cigar box
lids for paddles, and champagne
corks for balls to play a mini
version of lawn tennis indoors
during bad weather.

sections.title: Page 5 · HISTORY
sections.body:
HISTORY

Early names included whiff-
waff and flim-flam. The term
"ping-pong" came from the
sound of the ball.

sections.title: Page 6 · HISTORY

Tennis” appeared on a board and dice game made by J.H.Singer
of New York

sections.title: Page 7 · HISTORY
sections.body:
HISTORY

Today:
Table tennis has been an Olympic sport
since 1988.
International competitions follow rules
established by the International Table
Tennis Federation (ITTF).
Table tennis is no longer simply a
recreational indoor game it is a hig -
speed professional sport and a widely
accessible activity for people of all ages.

sections.title: Page 10 · RACKET or PADDLE
sections.body:
RACKET or PADDLE

                    1. Wooden blade or blade

              The blade is the core of the racket and its main purpose is to
                  provide a surface for striking the ball. The blade is typically
             made from wood, but can also be made from other materials
                such as carbon fiber.

                    2. The rubbers

              The rubbers are the surfaces that make contact with the ball
               and provide spin and speed.

                    3. The sponge

              The sponge is a layer of material between the rubbers that
                  provides additional bounce and speed.

                    4. The handle

              The handle is the part of the racket that you hold onto, and it
                       is typically made from wood, plastic, or composite materials.

quality is typically marked by star
ratings ranging from 1-star (training) up

1. Place the ball on the open palm of the
free hand.
2. Toss the ball upward before striking it.

server's side and then on the receiver's side.
4. Keep the ball visible to the receiver during
the service action.

sections.title: Page 28 · 1. A match is normally played as best of an odd number
sections.body:
1. A match is normally played as best of an odd number
   of games, commonly best of 5 or 7.
2. A game is normally won by the first player or pair to
   reach 11 points, provided they lead by at least 2
   points.
3. At 10–10, play continues until one side has a 2-point
   advantage.
4. Players alternate serves every 2 points. At deuce (10–
   10), service alternates after each point.

sections.title: Page 29 · 5. A player scores a point when the opponent fails to make
sections.body:
5. A player scores a point when the opponent fails to make
a legal return or commits another fault.
6. During a rally, the ball generally must bounce once on
the opponent's side before being returned.
7. If a served ball touches the net but otherwise lands
correctly, it is a let and the serve is replayed.
8. In doubles, teammates must alternate hitting the ball.

Singles: one player against one player.
Doubles: two players against two players.

topspin, backspin, and sidespin can greatly change the

sections.title: Page 31 · TAKE NOTE

travels rapidly over a short distance.
Footwork and positioning: good positioning is just as important
as having strong strokes.
Sportsmanship: players should respect opponents, officials, and
the rules of the game.

flashcards.front: What is a class in Java?
flashcards.back: A blueprint or template used to create objects

flashcards.front: What is an object?
flashcards.back: An instance of a class

flashcards.front: Which Java keyword commonly creates an object?
flashcards.back: new

flashcards.front: Which best represents the state of an object?
flashcards.back: Fields or instance variables

flashcards.front: What represents the behavior of an object?
flashcards.back: Methods

flashcards.front: Two objects created from the same class must contain identical field values.
flashcards.back: False — Separate objects may have independent field values.

flashcards.front: In Student student1 = new Student(), what is student1?
flashcards.back: A reference variable

flashcards.front: What does Student() do in a new Student() expression?
flashcards.back: Calls the constructor

flashcards.front: One class can be used to create multiple separate objects.
flashcards.back: True — A class is a template; multiple instances can be created from it.

flashcards.front: What is another term for an object created from a class?
flashcards.back: instance

flashcards.front: What is the primary purpose of a Java constructor?
flashcards.back: Initialize an object’s state

flashcards.front: A Java constructor must have the same name as its class.
flashcards.back: True — The class and constructor names must match.

flashcards.front: What return type must a constructor declare?
flashcards.back: No return type

flashcards.front: Java constructors are inherited by subclasses in the same way instance methods are.
flashcards.back: False — The source explains that constructors are not inherited; super() may invoke a superclass constructor.

flashcards.front: What happens if no constructor is declared in a Java class?
flashcards.back: The compiler may provide a default no-argument constructor

flashcards.front: What distinguishes a programmer-written no-argument constructor from a compiler-provided default constructor?
flashcards.back: It is explicitly declared by the programmer

flashcards.front: What is constructor overloading?
flashcards.back: Multiple constructors with different parameter lists

flashcards.front: Changing only parameter names, while keeping parameter types and order, overloads a constructor.
flashcards.back: False — The parameter list types/order, not local names, determine overloads.

flashcards.front: Which keyword invokes another constructor in the same class?
flashcards.back: this

flashcards.front: Where must a this(...) constructor call appear?
flashcards.back: As the first statement in a constructor

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a copy constructor pattern?
flashcards.back: Initialize an object using values from another object

flashcards.front: Which statement about a static field is correct?
flashcards.back: It belongs to the class and is shared among instances

flashcards.front: What is the preferred way to access a public static field?
flashcards.back: Through the class name

flashcards.front: Which Java keyword refers to the current object?
flashcards.back: this

flashcards.front: A static method can directly access an instance variable without an object reference.
flashcards.back: False — A static method has no implicit instance to identify that field.

flashcards.front: Why is Java main() declared static?
flashcards.back: The JVM can invoke it without creating an instance first

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a static initialization block?
flashcards.back: Perform initialization when the class is initialized

flashcards.front: The this keyword can be used directly inside a static method.
flashcards.back: False — this requires a current object; a static context has none.

flashcards.front: Which member can a static method use directly?
flashcards.back: Another static member of the class

flashcards.front: What is globalization?
flashcards.back: Increasing interconnectedness and interdependence across the world

flashcards.front: Which perspective expects a single borderless world and reduced national-government power?
flashcards.back: Hyperglobalist

flashcards.front: Which perspective emphasizes nation-state continuity and doubts globalization is unprecedented?
flashcards.back: Skeptic / Anti-Globalist

flashcards.front: Which perspective argues states are reconfigured rather than simply disappearing?
flashcards.back: Transformationalist

flashcards.front: What term refers to global forces interacting with local contexts?
flashcards.back: glocalization

flashcards.front: The globalization reviewer describes globalization as including cultural exchange.
flashcards.back: True — Globalization encompasses more than trade, including cultural integration.

flashcards.front: What does GVC stand for?
flashcards.back: Global Value Chain

flashcards.front: What is global finance?
flashcards.back: Movement of money, capital and assets across borders

flashcards.front: Which group is highlighted as an example of Philippine cross-border labor migration?
flashcards.back: Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs)

flashcards.front: The reviewer says OFW remittances contribute to the Philippine economy.
flashcards.back: True — Remittances from OFWs bolster national economic output.

flashcards.front: What does BSP stand for?
flashcards.back: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas

flashcards.front: Which integration involves acquiring competitors at the same production level?
flashcards.back: Horizontal integration

flashcards.front: Which integration controls different stages of production or marketing?
flashcards.back: Vertical integration

flashcards.front: Which integration combines unrelated enterprises to diversify risk?
flashcards.back: Conglomerate integration

flashcards.front: Which type studies how efficiently prices transmit across geographic regions?
flashcards.back: Spatial market integration

flashcards.front: A firm acquiring direct competitors is an example of vertical integration.
flashcards.back: False — Acquiring competitors at the same production level is horizontal integration.

flashcards.front: What integration type combines unrelated businesses?
flashcards.back: conglomerate integration

flashcards.front: Which historical peace settlement is associated with the modern sovereign-state system?
flashcards.back: Peace of Westphalia (1648)

flashcards.front: Which combination defines the reviewer’s state concept?
flashcards.back: Territory, population, government and sovereignty

flashcards.front: Which idea best describes a nation in the reviewer?
flashcards.back: An imagined community sharing culture and history

flashcards.front: Which actor is listed as an intergovernmental organization?
flashcards.back: World Trade Organization (WTO)

flashcards.front: Which is named as a binding international treaty?
flashcards.back: Paris Agreement

flashcards.front: Contemporary global governance requires one world government to exist.
flashcards.back: False — The source explicitly defines it as collective management without one world government.

flashcards.front: What maritime treaty framework is mentioned in connection with the West Philippine Sea dispute?
flashcards.back: UNCLOS

flashcards.front: What does the Global North generally refer to in the reviewer?
flashcards.back: Wealthy, industrialized and technologically advanced nations

flashcards.front: Which region is the Philippines categorized under in this reviewer?
flashcards.back: Global South

flashcards.front: Which set best describes the ASEAN Way?
flashcards.back: Non-interference, consensus and informality

flashcards.front: What is Asian regionalism?
flashcards.back: Increasing economic, political and sociocultural integration among Asian nations

flashcards.front: The Philippines was a founding member of ASEAN in 1967.
flashcards.back: True — The reviewer names the Philippines as a founding ASEAN member.

flashcards.front: What regional grouping is characterized by consensus and non-interference?
flashcards.back: ASEAN

flashcards.front: What is sex-typing?
flashcards.back: Believing particular jobs suit men or women based on biological sex

flashcards.front: What is access discrimination?
flashcards.back: Difficulty entering a job field because of sex

flashcards.front: What is treatment discrimination?
flashcards.back: Unequal pay or promotion despite similar qualifications and performance

flashcards.front: What does the maternal wall refer to?
flashcards.back: Bias against mothers or pregnant employees in the workplace

flashcards.front: Which responsibility can limit women’s participation in paid work according to the reviewer?
flashcards.back: Disproportionate unpaid domestic work

flashcards.front: The reviewer says equal pay and adequate parental leave help address gender inequality at work.
flashcards.back: True — Work-family balance and equal opportunities support workplace equality.

flashcards.front: What term refers to stereotypes assigning careers as “masculine” or “feminine”?
flashcards.back: sex-typing

flashcards.front: Which two are identified as main pillars of gender socialization?
flashcards.back: Family and school

flashcards.front: What is gender socialization?
flashcards.back: Learning socially expected ways of behaving and thinking by sex

flashcards.front: What should gender-responsive educators encourage?
flashcards.back: Cross-gender interaction and counter-stereotypic examples

flashcards.front: What response to teacher bias does the reviewer support?
flashcards.back: Explicit training backed by school policy

flashcards.front: The reviewer recommends promoting egalitarian attitudes in co-educational schools.
flashcards.back: True — The source favors improving co-educational schools rather than default segregation.

flashcards.front: What is the process by which individuals learn gender norms from society?
flashcards.back: gender socialization

flashcards.front: What are gender stereotypes?
flashcards.back: Oversimplified beliefs about people based on gender

flashcards.front: Which source of gender norms is emphasized in the reviewer?
flashcards.back: Advertising and media

flashcards.front: The source says children may internalize gender stereotypes early.
flashcards.back: True — The reviewer describes the effect of stereotypes on young children.

flashcards.front: What is important for fair gender representation in media?
flashcards.back: Media pluralism and editorial freedom

flashcards.front: What term refers to oversimplified beliefs that members of a group are the same?
flashcards.back: stereotypes

flashcards.front: Where was pickleball created in 1965?
flashcards.back: Bainbridge Island, Washington

flashcards.front: Which group founded pickleball?
flashcards.back: Joel Pritchard, Bill Bell and Barney McCallum

flashcards.front: Which sports contributed elements to pickleball?
flashcards.back: Badminton, tennis and table tennis

flashcards.front: How many players are on each side during pickleball doubles?
flashcards.back: Two

flashcards.front: What area is commonly called the kitchen in pickleball?
flashcards.back: The non-volley zone

flashcards.front: In pickleball, how is a legal serve directed?
flashcards.back: Diagonally into the appropriate service court

flashcards.front: What does the two-bounce rule require?
flashcards.back: The serve and return must each bounce before a volley is allowed

flashcards.front: What is a dink in pickleball?
flashcards.back: A soft shot landing in or near the opponent’s non-volley zone

flashcards.front: What is a volley?
flashcards.back: Hitting the ball before it bounces

flashcards.front: What is a lob?
flashcards.back: A high shot over an opponent’s head

flashcards.front: What is a groundstroke?
flashcards.back: A stroke played after the ball bounces

flashcards.front: What grip is also called the handshake grip?
flashcards.back: Continental grip

flashcards.front: What is the pickleball term for the non-volley zone?
flashcards.back: kitchen

flashcards.front: Pickleball can be played indoors or outdoors.
flashcards.back: True — The definition mentions both locations.

flashcards.front: Which shot is described as a faster, more powerful groundstroke?
flashcards.back: Drive

Which international federation sets rules for table tennis competitions?
flashcards.back: ITTF

flashcards.front: Where did the Victorian indoor parlor version of ping-pong develop?
flashcards.back: England

flashcards.front: What is the standard table tennis ball diameter in the lecture?
flashcards.back: 40 millimeters

flashcards.front: How much does the standard table tennis ball weigh?
flashcards.back: 2.7 grams

flashcards.front: How many points normally win a game of table tennis, with a two-point lead?
Which table tennis stroke is a powerful attacking shot?

flashcards.front: Which stroke uses the racket to redirect a fast incoming shot with minimal swing?
flashcards.back: Block

flashcards.front: Which stroke is described as a soft, controlled defensive return?
flashcards.back: Push

flashcards.front: Which is a table tennis footwork technique named in the lecture?

flashcards.front: In singles table tennis, how many players face each other?
flashcards.back: One player against one

flashcards.front: The table tennis lecture describes reaction time as an important skill.
flashcards.back: True — Reaction time is highlighted due to ball speed.

flashcards.front: What is the abbreviation of the International Table Tennis Federation?
flashcards.back: ITTF

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of the ready position?
flashcards.back: Prepare to react quickly to incoming shots

flashcards.front: How should knees be positioned in the basic ready stance?
flashcards.back: Slightly bent

flashcards.front: Where should the player hold the racket in the ready stance?
flashcards.back: In front of the body

flashcards.front: How tightly should a player hold the racket?
flashcards.back: Firmly, but not excessively tight

flashcards.front: Which grip is often compared to holding a hammer?
flashcards.back: Continental grip

flashcards.front: What does footwork help a player do?
flashcards.back: Reach shots on time and recover position

flashcards.front: Which movement is explicitly listed as basic court footwork?
flashcards.back: Split step

flashcards.front: What is hand-eye coordination?
flashcards.back: Using visual information to guide hand and racket movement

flashcards.front: Which is a basic hand-eye coordination drill?
flashcards.back: Ball toss and catch

flashcards.front: Which stroke uses the dominant side of the body?
flashcards.back: Forehand

flashcards.front: Which stroke is performed on the non-dominant side?
flashcards.back: Backhand

flashcards.front: Which activity practices keeping the ball bouncing on the racket?
flashcards.back: Racket tapping

flashcards.front: A relaxed but alert posture is recommended in the ready position.
flashcards.back: True — The slide recommends being relaxed and alert.

flashcards.front: What is the ability to guide hand movements using visual information called?
flashcards.back: hand-eye coordination
